title: Middleware Concepts
description: Understand the middleware pipeline in ASP.NET Core, how requests flow through components, and how to compose middleware to handle cross-cutting concerns like logging, authentication, and error handling.

blocks.text: In ASP.NET Core, middleware are software components that are assembled into an application pipeline to handle requests and responses. Each middleware component can decide whether to pass the request to the next component in the pipeline or short-circuit the chain.

Think of middleware like stations on an assembly line. A request enters at the first station, and each station can inspect, modify, or reject the request before passing it along. When the response comes back, it flows back through the same stations in reverse order.

blocks.title: Pipeline Analogy
blocks.text: The middleware pipeline is similar to an onion. Requests travel from the outermost layer inward to reach your endpoint, and responses travel back outward. This is why ordering middleware matters so much.
How Requests Flow Through the Pipeline

When a browser or API client sends an HTTP request to your ASP.NET Core application, it does not land directly on your controller action. Instead, it passes through a series of middleware components before reaching its destination. Each component can:

blocks.title: What middleware can do with a request
items: Handle the request entirely and return a response without calling the next middleware (short-circuiting)
Perform work before the request reaches the endpoint, such as logging or authentication
Perform work after the endpoint has produced a response, such as compression or caching headers
Pass the request to the next middleware in the chain using the 'next' delegate

blocks.text: The pipeline is built in the order you register middleware. A component registered first sees the request first and sees the response last. This ordering is one of the most important concepts to understand when working with ASP.NET Core.

Every middleware component receives a 'next' delegate as a parameter. This delegate represents the next middleware in the pipeline. Calling 'await next()' passes control to the next component. If you never call 'next()', the pipeline stops, and the request never reaches your endpoint.

blocks.title: Inline middleware using a lambda
blocks.content: This inline middleware logs the incoming request path before passing it to the next component.

blocks.text: In this example, the inline middleware writes a log line before and after calling 'next()'. The 'await next()' line is critical — without it, the request would never reach the MapGet endpoint, and the client would receive no response.

blocks.title: Tip: Use ILogger in real apps
blocks.text: In production applications, replace Console.WriteLine with the built-in ILogger<T> service. It supports structured logging, log levels, and integrates with monitoring platforms like Application Insights and Serilog.

The order in which you call UseMiddleware or extension methods like UseRouting and UseAuthentication is critical. Some middleware must come before others to function correctly. Here are the general rules:

blocks.title: Middleware ordering best practices
items: Exception handling and HTTPS redirection should be registered first so they catch issues from all downstream middleware
Static file serving should come early if you want files served without hitting the routing system
Routing must come before any middleware that needs to know which endpoint was matched
Authentication and authorization should come after routing but before endpoint execution
CORS middleware should be placed early in the pipeline to handle preflight requests

blocks.title: Warning: Order matters!
blocks.text: Putting UseAuthorization before UseAuthentication is a common mistake. Authentication runs first to establish who the user is. Authorization runs second to decide what that user can do. Swapping them will cause unexpected 401 and 403 errors.

terms.definition: A software component that processes HTTP requests and responses as part of the ASP.NET Core pipeline.
The ordered sequence of middleware components that every request passes through.
A function that calls the next middleware in the pipeline, represented by the 'next' parameter in middleware classes.
When middleware handles a request without calling next(), stopping further pipeline processing.
A middleware that does not call next(), effectively ending the pipeline and returning a response.

blocks.title: Terminal middleware that short-circuits
blocks.content: This middleware returns a response without ever calling next(), demonstrating short-circuiting.

blocks.title: Build a Simple Logging Middleware
blocks.description: Create an inline middleware that logs the HTTP method, path, and response status code for every request.
steps: Create a new ASP.NET Core MVC project using 'dotnet new mvc -n MiddlewareLab'
Open Program.cs and locate the WebApplication builder and app variable
Add an inline middleware before app.MapControllers() that logs the HTTP method and path using Console.WriteLine
Inside the middleware, call 'await next()' to continue the pipeline
After next() returns, read context.Response.StatusCode and log it
Run the app with 'dotnet run' and test with a browser or curl to see logs in the terminal
blocks.expectedOutcome: The console terminal shows log lines for every incoming request showing the method, path, and response status code, proving the middleware is intercepting both the request and response.

items.hint: Think of middleware as software between the raw HTTP request and your controller actions.

items.text: I understand the 'next' delegate and why 'await next()' is critical
items.hint: Without calling next(), the request never reaches the endpoint.

items.text: I know the difference between short-circuiting and passing through middleware
items.hint: Short-circuiting means the middleware returns a response without calling next().

items.hint: The lambda receives HttpContext and a RequestDelegate called next.

items.hint: First registered middleware runs first and sees responses last.

blocks.title: Middleware Pipeline Summary
points: Middleware components form a chain that every HTTP request passes through before reaching an endpoint
Each middleware can perform work before and after calling next()
Short-circuiting happens when a middleware returns a response without calling next()
Registration order is critical: middleware runs in the order it is added
The 'next' delegate is what passes control to the following middleware component
Common use cases include logging, authentication, authorization, and CORS handling
blocks.takeaway: The middleware pipeline is the backbone of ASP.NET Core request processing. Understanding how components are ordered and how the 'next' delegate flows control through the pipeline is essential for building robust web applications.
